posts.author: UmbrotheUmbreon
posts.body:
So over the course of my time dabbling in RPG Maker engines, I've gained a lot of knowledge on how things work, as well as even been brave enough to delve into coding itself (it did not last long lol). I won't deny that I've never really pushed past ideas and gotten into an actual project, but I love games so much and enjoy the feeling of making something. While designing and trying things, I eventually learned how to use variables to a small degree.
However, one thing constantly plagued me while trying things out. I'd sit there and plan things out like "I could do this, but it might require its own variable" or "how can I utilize multiple things under the same variable condition?" It got me concerned if I was using too many variables, or trying to do too much. Eventually I struggled to understand if it was good to have tons of variables for random things.
The question I want to discuss is how many is too many? Is it reasonable, if not expected, to use literally hundreds of different variables? Is it possible to slim down a lot of things in game designing to not use so many variables? These are the questions I'd like to get more input and thoughts on from others.

posts.author: Timeline_man
posts.body:
there are really only two objective points when it is "too many"
It affects the performance of the game. This will only happen if everything is loaded on one map, generally speaking
You want to use more than the engine will allow you to add. I think in the case of MV specifically, that number is 2000?
It's important to remember that players generally won't see how "inefficiently" you built the game, and won't care so long as every part of it works. Use what you need to do what you want. I know my first big project used, like, 7 variables, but somewhere around 100 switches.
My general advice would be that the more things reference and/or change the same variable, the more likely you are to create a bug where variables are at unexpected values, so using a new variable for a new thing is unlikely to be a
bad
idea, in most cases.

Why would you need a separate variable for each amount of required material? I don’t know what crafting system your doing but if it’s just a checklist one..
You could just have a variable for the “craft item ID” of what your making and like 8 temp variables for the materials (4 for their “IDs” and 4 for the quantities of each) and a common event call with a list of conditional branches that would, based on what “Craft Item ID” set the other 8 variables to the item your choosing to make. You’d be using “set variable” because those requirements are constant and don’t need to be a dynamic variable.
But idk if that’s what kind of sys you meant.

posts.author: Zia_
posts.body:
I'm at 1500 variables in my project right now, but that has basically no significance in quality or scale of the game.
I always prefer clearly named variables with clear purposes, so I'd never recommend, to use "temp" or "trash" variables used for different occasions. You never know how your game will turn out, and your features might be available when you didn't expect it in the first place, so these "temp" things might be active at the same time. There's no benefit to it.
But, if you plan features that need a lot of values, you should consider to use variables for more than a single value.
For example, if you have 100 characters with 10 stats each, that would occupy 1000 variables. Instead, you can save these stats as arrays, so you need only one variable per character. This will need some scripting.
Also, you could save stats like these directly into the save file. This will require a plugin or scripting aswell. For example, in my game every character can be friends with everyone. That will make up to 20000+ combinations. I don't use variables for that.

•make a conditional branch that checks if you have the “dragon fangs” item in inventory
•if yes, then set a variable (name it “MatAmount” or something) to the amount of “dragon fangs” (in game data operand in variable operations)
•put another conditional branch under that which asks if variable “MatAmount” is equal to or greater than 3
•copy this whole thing and paste it inside that “yes if variable “MatAmount” is 3 or more section, and in this copied one edit it to check for wood item, wood item amount, and if variable “MatAmount” is 10 or more
•repeat this for 50 ash piles and 1 Flame Sword rank 1
•in the last conditional branch “if yes” part, use the “change items/change weapons” to remove the amounts of each item and weapon
•add Flame Sword rank 2 with “change weapons”

UmbrotheUmbreon said:
That's a lot of variables, but I guess in the grand scheme of things not really a lot if it doesn't hinder the game.
Click to expand...
There's not much of a hinderance to worry about. Variables store values for you, so don't hesitate to store what you need. Having 5 or 5000 variables in use* isn't much of a difference.
*while "in use" is also relative. Variables won't do anything if you don't interact with them codewise. Most of the time, they are just sitting in their shelf, holding their number and doing nothing but waiting for a call to add +1 or display the value in a textmessage.
What you might be concerned about are parallel process events. Too many of those, and if performed poorly, can affect the performance of the game by a lot.
And in many cases, parallel events can be avoided, if you have a good concept of what they are doing.
For example: You have a time feature in your game and display some kind of clock in your HUD. You could set up a parallel process, that always checks the current time and shows the correct information. But you could also call this check when your ingame time actually changes. There has to be some event that adds +1 to the ingame timer. That would be the right spot to check necessary HUD updates aswell.

No worries. It's actually nothing the RPG Maker would teach us on it's own. Not sure if there's a clean Tutorial about it. I learned about arrays in variables in this forum between the lines, and it was eye opening. I think
@AquaEcho
was talking about it somewhere.
I can give you a few examples how I use arrays in my game. But I'm not the best to explain the scripting, as I just figured out the situations I needed in particular. But others with more coding experience will help with specific questions, I'm sure.
Basically, an Array is a set of information, like:
[1, 5, 14, 17]
or
["Apple", "Herbs", "Potion"]
or
["Apple",2,"Herbs",10] ...
I have an array in a variable that holds all ActorIDs of actors, you have unlocked so far. So I can always use this to check, whichs actors are available for cutscenes, events or other stuff.
I can pick random numbers from the Array for randomized events.
A different array holds stat resistances and weaknesses like:
[1,0,-1,0,0,0,-1,1]
for every character. By script I can tell the game, which position belongs to which element, so it knows "resistant to fire, but weak to ice".
And you can also put text in it to be displayed in textmessages etc. E.g., you have something like:
["Chapter 1", "Chapter 2", "Chapter 3"]
And display these in a menu to click through the given options you want to read about.
You can tell the game by script "if you click right, take the next entry in the array. If you click left, take the previous. If you reach the end of array, go to the start/end and continue."
I could go on, but I hope, this gives a basic impression.

Yeah I actually discovered something similar to this through RPG Maker 2003. I tested the idea of using items as currency (so having an item be money for a certain NPC). I had a variable set to the amount of an item in the player's inventory (ItemSell), then have them input a number. That number was tied to a variable labeled "ItemBuy". If the chosen number equaled or was less than what the player owned, it would remove that much of the item, and you'd buy that much of the item the NPC sold you. That's actually how the original question of this post came about. I came to realize if I did this for EVERY item in the game, that might become too much.
